nameStory: The Atlantic Sergeant Major gets its military name from the distinctive dark vertical stripes across its yellow body, which resemble the chevron stripes on a sergeant's uniform. Like a stern military officer keeping order, this feisty damselfish is known for aggressively defending its territory on tropical reefs.
description: The Atlantic Sergeant Major is a small, oval-shaped tropical fish that's quite rare in New England waters. This bright yellow damselfish sports bold black vertical stripes running down its compressed body, making it look like it's wearing a military uniform. It typically grows to about 6-9 inches long and has a deep, disc-like body shape typical of reef fish.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright yellow body with 5-6 bold black vertical bars running from top to bottom - the pattern is so crisp it looks painted on

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, oval, and compressed from side to side like a dinner plate standing on edge - feels firm and muscular if handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single continuous dorsal fin along the back with spiny front rays that feel sharp to the touch, and a distinctly forked tail fin

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Palm-sized fish reaching up to 9 inches, about the length of a dollar bill

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the head, designed for picking at small prey and algae

habitat: In New England, this is an extremely rare visitor found only in the warmest coastal waters during late summer. Any sighting would likely be in shallow, rocky areas or around jetties where the water has been heated by the Gulf Stream. This tropical species is far outside its normal range when found in New England waters.

seasonality.spring: Not present in New England waters - too cold for this tropical species.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare visitor only in the warmest coastal waters during heat waves when Gulf Stream waters push northward.
seasonality.fall: Any stragglers from summer would quickly disappear as water temperatures drop below their tolerance.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent - cannot survive New England's cold winter waters.

funFact: Despite being called 'sergeant major,' these fish are actually more like underwater gardeners - the males carefully tend algae farms on rocks, weeding out unwanted species and fertilizing their crop with fish waste to feed their developing eggs!
confusionNotes: The bold yellow and black striped pattern is so distinctive that it's unlikely to be confused with any native New England fish. The closest might be a young cunner, but cunners lack the bright yellow color and crisp vertical stripes.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a Caribbean and tropical Atlantic species, so any sighting in New England would be extremely noteworthy and should be reported to local marine biologists. It represents the northern edge of climate-driven range expansion.
compareHints: The Atlantic Sergeant Major is much more brightly colored than its relative the Night Sergeant, which is darker with less distinct stripes. Among damselfishes, it's one of the most boldly patterned with its crisp yellow and black bars, while most other family members have more muted colors or different patterns entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative the Atlantic Sergeant Major, the Night Sergeant lacks the distinctive bright yellow body with bold black vertical stripes that make the Atlantic species instantly recognizable.
